Going Home

An AI agent app that turns hospital discharge papers into a plan a family can follow: a medicine timetable, phone reminders, a warning-signs card and questions for the doctor, in the family's language, with every dose checked against the original.

AuthorKush Dhall
GitHub repohttps://github.com/kush-kd/going-home
AppRuns locally from the repo (python run.py, then http://localhost:8000). Live mode runs on a Claude subscription through the Claude Code CLI. On a computer without a Claude login it starts in a clearly labeled demo mode that replays nine real recorded runs. A demo video is included.

2. Motivation

Who has the problem. Families bringing someone home from the hospital, and the person who becomes the caregiver overnight. Take Mr. Chen (one of our synthetic cases), 79, discharged after a mini-stroke caused by a new irregular heartbeat. He goes home with two new medicines, two changed doses, two medicines he must stop (aspirin and a ginkgo supplement, both of which raise bleeding risk with his new blood thinner), five follow-up visits and tests, and a list of warning signs. His papers are written like real ones: "1 tab PO BID", "QHS", a clinical hospital course full of abbreviations. His daughter manages his care and reads simplified Chinese best.

How they deal with it today. A nurse goes over the papers at discharge, often in a hurry and sometimes through an interpreter, and the family takes the printout home. After that, the family is on its own with the paper, the patient portal (which shows the same text), a phone call to the pharmacy, or a chatbot that may get a dose wrong.

What it costs them.

  • About 1 in 5 patients (19% of 400) had an adverse event within weeks of discharge, and most were caused by medicines[1].
  • In a phone follow-up of discharged patients, 86% knew they had new medicines, but only 56% knew the doses and 64% knew what they were for[2].
  • 81% of 1,511 standard discharge instructions were written above the recommended sixth-grade reading level[3].
  • About 25 million people in the US have limited English proficiency[4]. In one Toronto study, 22% of limited-English patients with chronic conditions returned to the ED within 30 days, versus 15% of English speakers[5].

Why anyone should care. The plan already exists; it is in the papers. The failure is in the hand-off to the family. A missed "STOP aspirin" or a confused dose of a blood thinner can mean a bleed or a stroke. Closing that gap needs no new medicine, only a plan the family can understand and act on.

3. What is new here

I looked at what a family can use today.

Existing optionWhat it does wellWhat it does not do
Patient portal / printed After Visit Summary (e.g., Epic MyChart)The official record, always availableSame hard text and abbreviations; no timetable; usually English only
Medication reminder apps (e.g., Medisafe)[8]Good reminders, caregiver alertsEvery medicine, dose and time is typed in by hand; nothing reads the discharge papers or checks them
General chatbots (ChatGPT and similar)Can explain a photo of the papers in many languagesNo check that doses match the source; no schedule, calendar or print chart; can invent facts
Machine translation (Google Translate)Fast, many languagesTranslates jargon literally; no plan; no safety checks
Hospital-side generative AI (Epic features; research tools)[7][9]Plain-language summaries for clinicians to reviewBuilt for the hospital, not the family at home; studies found omissions, inaccuracies and medicines not in the source[6]

What Going Home does differently, and why it matters:

  • Verification, not just generation. Every medicine, dose, frequency, date and phone number must be found word-for-word in the original document before it can reach the family. Research on AI discharge summaries found exactly the failure this prevents: omissions and invented medicines[6].
  • Actions, not just words. A day-by-day timetable with tick boxes (including steroid tapers and course end dates), one calendar file with every dose and visit, and a printable weekly chart.
  • It asks instead of guessing. Orders like "take as directed" or "resume home medications" become questions for the doctor.
  • Family-side and multilingual. Nine languages, with the English source sentence one tap away for the care team to check.

Honest limits on novelty: each ingredient (translation, plain language, reminders) exists somewhere. The new part is putting them together with a verification layer that makes the output safe enough to act on.

4. The agents

Figure 1. Going Home's pipeline. Teal boxes are Claude agents; dashed boxes are plain Python.

AgentWhat it doesTools and inputsModel and why
Transcriber (photos only)Copies every line of a photo or scanned page into textThe image; no other toolsSonnet: vision transcription is straightforward
ReaderExtracts medicines (status, strength, dose, schedule, taper steps, dates, daily maximums), appointments, warning groups, instructions and unclear items into a strict schema, each with an exact source_quoteThe cleaned document, fenced as untrusted data; JSON schema outputOpus: accuracy matters most here; it is the one step where a mistake becomes a wrong dose
CheckerIndependently compares the plan with the document: missed medicines, wrong values, a stopped medicine shown as active, missing warningsReal tools from an MCP server it calls itself: list_medication_lines, search_document, check_quote, verify_item; must quote the document for every problemSonnet: a second, different model gives an independent view at lower cost
ExplainerWrites everything in plain language at about a 5th-grade level, in the chosen language, plus translated labels for the screenOnly the verified, structured plan; never the raw documentSonnet: strong multilingual writing at lower cost

Tools the Checker calls. The Checker runs its own tool loop through an MCP server (app/mcp_tools.py) that the orchestrator starts for each review, loaded with that run's document and plan. It may call only those four tools, and a hard dollar cap applies to the call. Every tool call is logged and shown in the app. In the Chinese run below it made 5 calls:

#Tool the Checker calledInputResult
1list_medication_lines9 lines
2verify_itemm6{"verified": true, "score": 1.0, "problems": []}
3verify_itemm3{"verified": true, "score": 1.0, "problems": []}
4verify_itema3{"verified": true, "score": 1.0, "problems": []}
5check_quoteBring the log to{"found": true, "match": 1.0}

Steps the orchestrator runs in plain Python (no AI): the safety screen (file limits, hidden-text removal, prompt-injection removal); the grounding check (every quote must be in the document, and every number in a field must be in its quote); the scheduler (turns verified medicines into clock times and a calendar file); and the number check (any explained text with a number not in the verified data is replaced by the doctor's exact words).

How they are organized. A fixed pipeline with one controlled loop. The orchestrator runs the Reader, applies the grounding check, then starts the Checker and the Explainer in parallel: the Explainer usually does not need to wait. If the grounding check or the Checker finds a problem, the Reader gets one repair round with the exact problems listed, and the Explainer restarts on the fixed plan. Anything still unresolved is kept off the timetable and shown to the family as "check with your care team". A fixed pipeline fits this job better than free-form agent chat: every step is predictable, auditable and capped.

Per user and at scale

A "user" here is a family. Discharges are occasional, so I assume 2 plans per user per month (the first plan plus one re-run, for example in a second language or after a medication change). That is generous for one family; a hospital deploying it would pay per discharge instead.

Users (families)Plans per monthTokens per monthCost per month (API list prices)
1291,398$0.40
1002009,139,800$39.52
10,00020,000913,980,000$3,952.00

Per user per month: about $0.40. For a 300-bed hospital with roughly 15,000 discharges a year (an estimate), one plan per discharge would cost about $2,964 a year at API list prices, well under the cost of one full-time staff member.

What I did to keep cost down

  • Right model per job: Opus only for the Reader; Sonnet for the Checker, Explainer and Transcriber.
  • Compact inputs: the Explainer gets the verified structured plan, not the document.
  • Prompt caching: static system prompts are cached. Running the same safety-test file twice dropped from $0.146 to $0.086 (8,270 cached tokens on the second run).
  • Parallel, speculative Explainer: it runs alongside the Checker instead of after it, which saves time on most runs.
  • Repairs only when a check fails, capped at one round; and the second Checker pass is skipped when only the free, code-based grounding check flagged items.
  • Tools for the Checker: with the same prompts, giving the Checker tools cut the average cost from $0.250 to $0.198 per plan and repair rounds from 1 of 5 to 0 of 5. It verifies the doubtful items with code instead of re-reading and re-arguing everything.
  • Prompt fixes from real runs: the first eval needed a repair round on 2 of 4 cases; after tightening the prompts and checks, the final eval needed it on 0 of 5.

Did cost cutting hurt quality? An experiment

I ran the full pipeline with the cheaper Sonnet model as the Reader and compared it with the Opus Reader against the same answer key.

Reader modelPromptsCasesMedicines foundField accuracyFirst-read problems caughtRepair roundsAvg cost
Opusfinal5100%100%00/5$0.198
Sonnetfinal5100%100%11/5$0.182
Sonnetbefore fixes4100%100%62/4$0.226

Both final setups ran on the same five cases with the same prompts, checks and tool-using Checker.

Answer: not in final accuracy. With the final prompts and the tool-using Checker, the Sonnet Reader matched the Opus Reader on every medicine and field, at 8% lower cost, but needed 1 repair round(s) where Opus needed 0. Before I tightened the prompts, the same Sonnet Reader paraphrased instructions and once invented an "8 days" duration for the steroid taper. The grounding check caught every one of those, but each cost an extra repair round. The prompt fixes and the Checker's tools closed most of the gap.

My choice: I kept Opus as the Reader. The Reader is the one step where a mistake becomes a wrong dose, the cost difference is now small ($0.016 per plan), and Opus needed no repairs. Setting READER_MODEL=sonnet switches to the cheaper setup if a hospital needs it at scale; at 10,000 families it would save about $314 a month. Run times are not compared, because the evaluations ran at the same time as other jobs.

6. Safety

RiskWhat I builtEvidence
Prompt injection hidden in a PDF (white or tiny text)Removed by code before any agent reads the file, then shown to the userSafety-test sample (screenshot below); automated test
Visible injection ("AI assistant: ignore your checks")Whole sentence removed, even when it wraps across lines; the document is fenced as untrusted data in every prompt; the Explainer never sees itScreenshot; tests
Agent invents or mistypes a doseGrounding check on every quote and number; one repair round; unverified items never reach the timetableTests (wrong dose, invented quote, wrong frequency); real runs (repairs above)
Explainer adds a number or adviceNumber check on every explained card, in any script (e.g., Hindi digits); fallback to the doctor's wordsTests; caught real false alarms that I then fixed
Checker invents a problemIts claims must quote the document, or they are thrown outTest
Loops foreverAt most 1 repair round and 8 model calls per plan; the Checker's tool loop runs under a hard per-call dollar cap and may use only its four toolsTest (repair that never succeeds stops after one round)
Overspending150,000-token cap per plan; a hard --max-budget-usd cap on every agent call; 40 plans per day; 10 MB and 10-page upload limits; timeoutsTests for the token, call and daily caps. In real life, the daily cap stopped my own recording script on its 41st plan of the day.
Unsafe output in the pageEvery model or document string is escaped before displayCode review
PrivacyPapers are processed in memory and not stored; logs keep token counts only, no text or namesCode

A safety lesson from testing. My first injection filter also removed a real instruction from the Chinese case: "Aspirin 81 mg tab: STOP. You are now on apixaban". "You are now" is a common attack phrase. Dropping a STOP instruction is exactly the harm the app exists to prevent, so I narrowed the patterns and added a regression test that real sentences like this, and "your physician assistant should call you", are never removed. The full suite has 30 automated tests that run without any AI calls, including direct tests of the Checker's tools and of demo mode.

A simulated reader study (AI personas, not real people)

As a proxy before a real-user test, three AI personas (played by Claude Haiku) each answered six questions a caregiver must get right, once from the original papers and once from the Going Home plan in their language. Claude Sonnet graded every answer against my answer key (1, ½ or 0 points).

Simulated reader (AI persona)Plan languageFrom the original papersFrom the Going Home plan
Mei (daughter, reads Chinese)中文 (Chinese, Simplified)5 / 65.5 / 6
Rosa (sister, reads Spanish)Español (Spanish)5.5 / 64.5 / 6
Tom (husband, English, no medical background)English5.5 / 66 / 6
Total16 / 1816 / 18

What it shows, honestly: the overall scores tie. The plan clearly helped in one place: the daughter could not tell which medicines her father takes in the evening from the papers ("short words like BID and QHS that I don't understand") but could from the plan. Most other lost points came from strict grading of incomplete answers. It also flagged one translation nuance worth a human check: "blue lips" became labios morados, the natural Spanish phrase, which reads back as "purple". The big limitation: an AI persona reads English well even when told not to, so this proxy cannot show the main benefit (language and shorthand). That is why a real-user test matters. The full answers and grades are in docs/results/simulated_readers.json.

8. Limits and next steps

What doesn't work yet

  • Evaluation size: 5 synthetic cases plus one attack case. Real discharge papers vary more (scans, handwriting, multi-page tables).
  • Default clock times: "twice daily" becomes 8 AM and 8 PM (or with meals). The family can move them, but the app does not ask.
  • No drug-interaction or dose-safety knowledge: by design it only restates the papers. If the papers contain an error, the app repeats it faithfully.
  • Speed: one to three minutes per plan, longer in scripts like Hindi that use more output tokens.
  • Access: live mode runs on a Claude subscription through the Claude Code CLI, so other people need their own login; without one, demo mode replays recorded real runs but cannot read new papers.
  • Evidence of impact: beyond my own tests, the user evidence so far is a simulated reader study, which has clear limits (above).

What I would build next, with another month

  • A pilot with a hospital's discharge nurses: the nurse reviews the plan at the bedside before the family leaves (a human in the loop).
  • Read-back checks: the app asks the caregiver three questions ("what do you stop?") and flags wrong answers to the care team.
  • SMS reminders and a shared caregiver view; refill and lab-date nudges.
  • A larger evaluation on de-identified real discharge papers, including photos and scans.
  • Hosting with per-hospital billing, for families without a computer.
